notes: Complete EWCA Crim judgment on jurisdiction to entertain prosecution appeal from preparatory hearing ruling in van Hoogstraten retrial.

enrichment.short_title: Prosecution denied leave to appeal preparatory ruling that van Hoogstraten could not lawfully be convicted of manslaughter
key_facts: Nicholas van Hoogstraten was acquitted of murder but convicted of manslaughter over Mohammed Raja's killing; the Court of Appeal quashed that conviction in July 2003 and ordered a retrial for manslaughter only.

At a preparatory hearing Sir Stephen Mitchell ruled that, even on the agreed Crown case, no jury could properly convict van Hoogstraten of manslaughter because the fatal shooting was not an act he foresaw under Powell and English.

The prosecution sought leave to appeal that ruling under section 35(1) of the 1996 Act; the Court of Appeal held it had no jurisdiction because the application was not made for a purpose within section 29(2).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application by the prosecution for leave to appeal against a trial judge's preparatory hearing ruling on a question of law.
enrichment.outcome: Prosecution application refused; no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: A ruling at a preparatory hearing under section 31(3) of the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996 is appealable under section 35(1) only if it was made for one of the statutory purposes in section 29(2); an application whose object is to stop the trial proceeding, even if framed as a question of law, falls outside the ambit of the preparatory hearing and cannot be appealed by the prosecution.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge's ruling on manslaughter liability was a section 31(3) ruling appealable under section 35(1)
Whether an application to prevent trial proceeding falls within the purposes of a preparatory hearing under section 29(2)
Application of Powell and English foresight test to agreed facts (at trial judge level, not finally decided on appeal)

notes: Complete EWCA Crim CCRC reference judgment quashing murder conviction and giving provocation direction guidance after Smith (Morgan).

enrichment.short_title: Murder conviction quashed where psychiatric evidence on provocation was not put before jury pre-Smith (Morgan)
key_facts: Philip Rowland stabbed his wife Linda to death during a domestic argument in October 1995; he pleaded guilty to manslaughter by provocation at trial but the Crown proceeded on murder and he was convicted in February 1997.

Fresh psychiatric evidence from Dr McClelland and Dr McGuire, obtained on a second CCRC reference, showed clinical depression and over-controlled personality traits affecting his capacity for self-control.

At trial the judge directed the jury on provocation using the pre-Smith (Morgan) reasonable-man formula limited to age, sex and Peyronie's disease; expert evidence on depression and personality was not called.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following CCRC reference based on change in provocation law after R v Smith (Morgan).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; murder conviction quashed and substituted with manslaughter by reason of provocation; seven-year sentence substituted for life imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Where fresh psychiatric evidence shows that, under the law as clarified in Smith (Morgan), the jury should have been invited to consider the appellant's personality and depression when assessing whether his loss of self-control was sufficiently excusable, a murder conviction may be unsafe even though the trial summing-up was unexceptionable at the time; judges should use the Judicial Studies Board specimen direction and discuss provocation directions with counsel before speeches.
legal_issues: Admissibility and effect of fresh psychiatric evidence on the defence of provocation after Smith (Morgan)
Whether the trial judge's provocation direction was unsafe in light of evidence not before the jury
Proper approach to summing-up on characteristics and self-control following Weller and Smith (Morgan)

notes: Complete EWCA Civ immigration appeal dismissing judicial review of IAT refusal of leave to appeal on Albanian domestic violence asylum claim.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal dismissed where adjudicator found sufficient state protection for domestic violence victims in Albania
key_facts: The appellant, an Albanian national, claimed asylum based on domestic violence by her former partner Mr Koleci and threats from his family if returned to Albania.
The adjudicator heard state-protection material as a preliminary issue before credibility evidence and found sufficient protection available in Albania for women in her position.
Judicial review challenged the IAT's refusal of leave to appeal; Harrison J dismissed the claim and the Court of Appeal upheld that decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; removal directions and refusal of asylum upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Sufficiency of state protection under Horvath must be assessed in the light of the individual claimant's case; where the adjudicator took the claimant's account at face value and properly applied Horvath, a Wednesbury challenge to his conclusion on country material pointing in different directions will fail; adjudicators should be wary of deciding state protection as a preliminary issue in isolation.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred by determining state protection before hearing credibility evidence
Whether the adjudicator applied Horvath correctly to Albania domestic violence material
Whether Harrison J mischaracterised the nature of the feared harm on return

notes: Complete EWCA Civ environmental appeal holding deep well injection of liquid hazardous waste constitutes landfill under 2002 Regulations.

enrichment.short_title: Deep borehole injection of imported liquid hazardous waste held to be landfill under Landfill Regulations 2002
key_facts: Blackland Park operated the Whisby oilfield in Lincolnshire and injected large quantities of imported liquid hazardous waste into deep sandstone and limestone strata via a borehole.
Regulation 9(1) of the Landfill Regulations absolutely prohibits acceptance of liquid waste at landfill sites from July 2002; landfill is defined as disposal of waste onto or into land.
Blackburne J granted a declaration that the site was a landfill for imported liquid wastes; the company was said to be the only UK operator using this disposal method.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against High Court declaration under CPR Part 40.20 on lawfulness of continued deep injection operations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; site held to be a landfill and subject to the liquid waste prohibition; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Disposal of imported hazardous liquid waste by injection into deep underground strata where the waste remains within a defined geological reservoir constitutes deposit of waste into land and therefore landfill within regulation 3(2) and Article 2(g) of the Landfill Directive; the distinction between deposit and discharge does not exclude such operations, and overlap with groundwater legislation does not render the Landfill Directive inapplicable.
legal_issues: Whether deep well injection of liquid waste is landfill within the Landfill Regulations and Directive
Whether deposit differs from discharge into groundwater for regulatory purposes
Whether Annex I technical standards show the activity was never intended to be regulated as landfill
Whether declaratory proceedings were appropriate in exceptional circumstances

notes: Complete EWCA Crim CCRC reference judgment quashing Pinfold and MacKenney murder convictions based on unreliable accomplice evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Historic murder convictions quashed where accomplice Childs's evidence held wholly unreliable on fresh psychiatric evidence
key_facts: Terence Pinfold and Henry MacKenney were convicted in 1980 of murders linked to John Bruce Childs, who had pleaded guilty to six murders and gave evidence against co-accused.

The jury convicted only where Childs's evidence was corroborated; fresh evidence included psychiatric opinions that Childs suffered severe personality disorder making his testimony wholly unreliable, plus post-trial retractions.
The CCRC referred the convictions in 2001; retrial was not viable decades later and Childs could not give evidence again.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following CCRC reference on fresh medical and retraction evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; convictions quashed as unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 23 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968 the Court of Appeal may admit expert psychiatric evidence on a witness's credibility without physical examination of the witness, going to weight not admissibility; applying Pendleton, where fresh evidence shows an accomplice's evidence is so unreliable that corroboration cannot save convictions depending on it, the convictions are unsafe even though the jury were warned and the summing-up was fair.
legal_issues: Admissibility of psychiatric expert evidence on witness credibility without examining the witness
Effect of post-trial retractions by an accomplice witness
Whether convictions were safe where jury convicted only on corroborated counts
Application of Pendleton test to fresh evidence on CCRC reference

notes: Complete EWCA Civ judgment on civil no case to answer procedure and Wisniewski adverse inferences.

enrichment.short_title: Estate agent's commission claim restored after judge wrongly upheld no case to answer without putting defendants to election
key_facts: Benham & Reeves claimed commission for acting as Kythira's agent in purchasing Leavesden Cottage and Spedan Cottages in Hampstead in 1998 through employee Jeremy Gee.
After four days of the claimants' evidence Judge Geddes entertained a no case to answer submission without putting the defendants to their election and dismissed the claim.

Circumstantial evidence included solicitors' letters referring to Benham & Reeves as the client's agents and Mr Gee's diary entries; Mr Gee was unavailable to give evidence after dismissal for misconduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against High Court order dismissing claim at close of claimants' evidence on no case to answer.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claim remitted for retrial before a different judge.
enrichment.ratio: Rarely should a civil trial judge entertain a submission of no case to answer without putting the defendant to election; if entertained, the test is whether the claimant has a real prospect of success or a prima facie case, not balance of probabilities, and the judge may consider that adverse inferences could strengthen a weak case if the defendant elects not to call material evidence (Wisniewski).
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have put the defendants to their election before ruling on no case to answer
Correct test when entertaining a no case submission at mid-trial
Relevance of adverse inference principles to no case submissions
Whether circumstantial evidence established a prima facie agency retainer

notes: Complete Admin Court judgment dismissing challenge to three-year football banning order after ticket touting conviction.

enrichment.short_title: Three-year football banning order upheld after conviction for unauthorised ticket sale at Arsenal match

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Lee Brown pleaded guilty to offering for sale a ticket for the designated Arsenal v Newcastle match on 9 November 2002 contrary to section 166 of the 1994 Act.
Highbury Corner magistrates imposed a three-year banning order under section 14A; Inner London Crown Court dismissed his appeal.
Undercover officers observed him touting tickets and he was found with over £426 cash; the minimum non-custodial banning period under section 14F was three years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review with leave of the single judge against Crown Court dismissal of appeal against a section 14A banning order.
enrichment.ratio: Section 14A and section 14B of the Football Spectators Act 1989 create distinct regimes: on conviction of a relevant offence the court must make a banning order if satisfied there are reasonable grounds to believe it would help prevent violence or disorder, without importing the section 14B requirement that the person has caused or contributed to violence; ticket touting is listed as a relevant offence because it undermines crowd control and increases disorder risk.
legal_issues: Whether section 14B(2) must be read into section 14A by implication
Whether a single ticket sale justified a banning order as proportionate
Whether reasonable grounds existed that the order would help prevent violence or disorder

notes: Complete EWCA Civ judgment on section 73 Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 certification in Balamurali and Sandhu.

enrichment.short_title: Court of Appeal defines legitimate purpose test for section 73 immigration appeal certification
key_facts: Balamurali, a Sri Lankan asylum claimant, received section 73 certificates after a further Article 8 human rights appeal following earlier dismissed appeals; the Secretary of State said the Article 8 claim could have been raised earlier and aimed to delay removal.
Sandhu's fresh Article 8 application after marriage and birth of a child was certified under section 73(8); a deputy judge quashed the certificate but the human rights refusal stood.
Conflicting High Court approaches had treated no other legitimate purpose as either a merits test or a pure delaying-tactic test.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals to the Court of Appeal against High Court judicial review decisions on section 73 certification under the 1999 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Balamurali appeal dismissed; Secretary of State's appeal allowed in Sandhu (certificate quashing reversed); permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused in Balamurali.
enrichment.ratio: Section 73 limits further immigration appeals after a finally determined original appeal: where the Secretary of State has rejected a fresh claim he may certify under section 73(8) or section 73(2) if one purpose is to delay removal and, in his opinion, the applicant had no other legitimate purpose beyond buying time; legitimate purpose is not simply a merits test but asks whether the applicant had some worthwhile reason such as a significant change in circumstances, though delay and ability to raise points earlier are relevant factors.
legal_issues: Meaning of no other legitimate purpose in section 73(2)(c) and section 73(8)(b)
Relationship between section 73(8) certification and subsequent notice of appeal certification under section 73(2)
Whether certification requires the claim to be manifestly unfounded or a pure delaying tactic
Correct approach to Article 8 claims raised after finally determined asylum/human rights appeals

notes: Complete EWCA Civ employment appeal allowing retrial where tribunal lay member consumed alcohol during hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Unfair dismissal claim remitted after employment tribunal lay member drank alcohol during hearing
key_facts: James Stansbury was dismissed for redundancy by Datapulse Plc in September 2000 and unsuccessfully claimed unfair dismissal before a Reading employment tribunal.
He alleged lay member Mr Eynon fell asleep and smelled strongly of alcohol during hearings in May and July 2001; the chairman acknowledged smelling alcohol on Mr Eynon's breath.
Counsel Mrs Kavanagh had not raised the issue at trial but later stated a panel member was plainly drunk; the EAT assumed alcohol consumption and possible sleep but held the hearing fair.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission on limited procedural grounds from Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissal of unfair dismissal appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal decision set aside; case remitted for rehearing before a differently constituted tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: A fair hearing requires each tribunal member to be alert and appear alert throughout; where a lay member has consumed alcohol to the extent that he appeared not to concentrate and may have fallen asleep, Article 6 and domestic fairness requirements are breached regardless of unanimous reserved reasons or prior EAT rejection on merits; the EAT must resolve disputed facts on tribunal misconduct when necessary, and failure to raise the point at trial is not necessarily a bar to appeal.
legal_issues: Whether failure to complain at the hearing prevents raising tribunal misconduct on appeal
EAT's function in resolving factual disputes about tribunal member conduct
Whether assumed drunkenness and sleep at a tribunal hearing can still be fair under Article 6
Appropriate remedy when tribunal member misconduct is established
